cards.claim: Multiplying a vector by a positive number lambda scales its magnitude by lambda and keeps its direction.
cards.quote: Multiplying a vector A with a positive number λ gives a vector whose magnitude is changed by the factor λ but the direction is the same as that of A

locator.section: 3.3 Multiplication of vectors by real numbers

cards.claim: Multiplying a vector by a negative number -lambda reverses its direction and multiplies its magnitude by lambda.
cards.quote: Multiplying a vector A by a negative number −λ gives another vector whose direction is opposite to the direction of A and whose magnitude is λ times |A|.

locator.section: 3.3 Multiplication of vectors by real numbers

cards.claim: The multiplier can carry its own physical dimension: the product's dimension is the product of the dimensions, e.g. a constant velocity times a time interval is a displacement.
cards.quote: Then, the dimension of λ A is the product of the dimensions of λ and A. For example, if we multiply a constant velocity vector by duration (of time), we get a displacement vector.

locator.section: 3.3 Multiplication of vectors by real numbers

cards.claim: The same-or-opposite-direction rule has an edge case: multiplying by zero gives the null vector, whose magnitude is zero and whose direction cannot be specified.
cards.quote: Since the magnitude of a null vector is zero, its direction cannot be specified. The null vector also results when we multiply a vector A by the number zero.

locator.section: 3.4 Addition and subtraction of vectors — graphical method

cards.claim: Multiplying A by 2 gives 2A, in the same direction as A with twice its magnitude (Fig. 3.3a).
cards.quote: For example, if A is multiplied by 2, the resultant vector 2A is in the same direction as A and has a magnitude twice of |A| as shown in Fig. 3.3(a).

locator.section: 3.3 Multiplication of vectors by real numbers

cards.claim: A negative multiplier does not give a negative magnitude: the magnitude of alpha*A is |alpha| times |A| (magnitudes are positive numbers); a negative alpha only makes the new vector antiparallel to A.
cards.quote: The magnitude | B → | | B → | of this new vector is obtained by multiplying the magnitude | A → | | A → | of the original vector, as expressed by the scalar equation : B = | α | A . B = | α | A . 2.2 In a scalar equation, both sides of the equation are numbers. Equation 2.2 is a scalar equation because the magnitudes of vectors are scalar quantities (and positive numbers). If the scalar α α is negative in the vector equation Equation 2.1 , then the magnitude | B → | | B → | of the new vector is still given by Equation 2.2 , but the direction of the new vector B → B → is antiparallel to the direction of A → A → .

locator.section: 2.1 Scalars and Vectors — Algebra of Vectors in One Dimension

cards.claim: NCERT Exercise 3.4 asks which algebraic operations between scalar and vector quantities are meaningful, including multiplying any vector by any scalar.
cards.quote: State with reasons, whether the following algebraic operations with scalar and vector physical quantities are meaningful : (a) adding any two scalars, (b) adding a scalar to a vector of the same dimensions , (c) multiplying any vector by any scalar, (d) multiplying any two scalars, (e) adding any two vectors, (f) adding a component of a vector to the same vector .

question.exam: NCERT Class XI Physics Part I textbook exercises
question.paper: Chapter 3 Motion in a Plane, Exercises (Reprint 2026-27)

cards.claim: NCERT answer to 3.4: only (c) multiplying any vector by any scalar and (d) multiplying any two scalars are permissible.

cards.quote: Read each statement below carefully and state, with reasons and examples, if it is true or false : A scalar quantity is one that (a) is conserved in a process (b) can never take negative values (c) must be dimensionless (d) does not vary from one point to another in space (e) has the same value for observers with different orientations of axes.
